decisions.reason: Zuboff herself contrasts automate and informate in the HBS interview and uses informating. This is a genuine English information-technology verb with a recognizable inform element, not an apparent spelling error. The exact -ed/-ing forms are regular finite morphological inferences from the attested verb; the interview directly attests informating. No invented corpus measurement or claim that HBS supplies a dictionary inflection table.

The product publisher uses the exact plural informationals for informational records; the student organization independently uses it for informational meetings. These are transparent nominal uses of informational from information. Rare noun morphology is attested rather than rejected as an apparent adjective error.

decisions.reason: The Dutch government defines and repeatedly uses informateur in its English explanation of government formation. This supplies target-language attestation of the borrowed lexical role, rather than an unexplained foreign quotation. The French information-provider head is separately dictionary-attested; the unchanged inform constituent remains recognizable. The source proves attested lexical usage, not every sense or corpus context.

The Duden Luxembourg Standard German publisher preview explicitly lists Informateur as a vocabulary item in the national variety. French informateur is documented as an information-provider head. This is evidence of a German national-variety lexical borrowing, not an instruction to accept all French insertions. Preview retrieval was available in indexed text; direct PDF open returned 406, so no unseen full dictionary entry is claimed.

Duden directly defines the German noun as a person working in an observatory and gives Latin observator as origin. Exact national lexical identity and observation branch are documented; no prefix conversion rule.

The digitized historical Italian-English dictionary explicitly gives osservamento as observation beside osservazione and osservare. The exact plural -i is a finite regular noun-inflection inference. The historical head has the transparent Italian osserv realization of observ; this does not claim frequent modern usage or an open osserv* classifier.

The historical dictionary equates informaggiare with incaciare; Treccani defines incaciare as seasoning with cheese. This is the independent formaggio/cheese branch, not an information verb. The two exact participles are finite regular morphology of this head. The shared inform letters cross the in- + formaggio boundary; no global inform exclusion.
